children.text: In the previous module, we encountered the spontaneous oxidation-reduction reaction between copper metal and an aqueous solution of silver nitrate. In this reaction, electrons were transferred from Cu to Ag

, but the energy produced by the reaction was lost to the surroundings as heat. How are we able to harness the electrical energy from this (and other) redox reactions? We do this by creating an electrochemical cell which separates the two half-reactions, thus allowing electrons to flow from the oxidation half-reaction to the reduction half-reaction through an external wire. Using a stack of copper and zinc disks separated by electrolyte layers, Alessandro Volta invented the first such device—the first battery—in 1800.
Galvanic cells
An electrochemical cell in which a spontaneous redox reaction takes place; also called a voltaic cell.
, also known as
voltaic cells

, are electrochemical cells in which spontaneous redox reactions produce electrical energy. (They are named in honor of Volta and the discoverer of bioelectricity, Luigi Galvani.) The batteries in your car, cell phone, laptop, flashlight, and so on, are all voltaic cells. The specifics of the electrochemical reactions in each of these battery types can vary significantly, but the principles of their design and operation are the same.
Let's start by considering a galvanic cell based on the reaction between copper and silver, as shown the image below. The cell consists of two half-cells, each containing the redox
conjugate pair
An acid–base pair in which the two substances differ by only one proton.
(“couple”) of a single reactant. The
half-cell
A part of an electrochemical cell where either the oxidation or reduction half-reaction occurs; it contains the redox conjugate pair (“couple”) of a single reactant.
on the left contains the Cu
/Cu couple in the form of a piece of copper metal partially submerged in an aqueous solution of copper(II) nitrate. The right half-cell contains the Ag
/Ag couple as silver metal in a silver nitrate solution. A wire is used to connect the metal pieces, which are called
electrodes
A conductor through which electricity enters or leaves an electrochemical cell; the anode is the electrode where oxidation occurs, and the cathode, where reduction occurs.
. An
active electrode
An electrode that participates as a reactant or product in the redox reaction of an electrochemical cell; the mass of an active electrode changes during the redox reaction.
participates in the redox reaction, whereas an
inert electrode
An electrode that conducts electrons to and from the reactants in a half-cell but that is not itself oxidized or reduced.
allows current to flow but does not participate in the redox reaction. The circuit is completed using a tube filled with inert electrolyte solution, known as a
salt bridge
The part of an electrochemical cell used to maintain electrical neutrality by allowing ion exchange between half-cells; usually a salt solution that prevents mixing and completes the circuit.

children.text: In this standard galvanic cell, the half-cells are separated; electrons can flow through an external wire and become available to do electrical work.

This device contains all the reactants and products of the copper-silver redox system but prevents physical contact between the reactants. Direct transfer of electrons is therefore prevented; instead, transfer takes place indirectly through an external circuit that connects the separated reactants.The oxidation half-reaction occurs at the surface of the Cu electrode in the half-cell on the left, and the electrode where oxidation occurs is known as the
anode
The electrode in an electrochemical cell where oxidation occurs; the site where electrons are released (from which electrons flow away).
. The reduction half-reaction occurs at the surface of the Ag electrode in the right half-cell; the electrode where reduction occurs is called the
cathode
The electrode in an electrochemical cell where reduction occurs; the site where electrons are gained (to which electrons flow toward).
. The anode is connected to a voltmeter with a wire, and the other terminal of the voltmeter is connected to the cathode by a wire.

When the two electrodes are first connected, current does not flow—that is, no significant movement of electrons through the wire occurs—because the circuit is open. The circuit is closed using a salt bridge, which transmits the current with moving ions. The salt bridge consists of a concentrated, nonreactive electrolyte solution such as the sodium nitrate (NaNO

) solution used in this example. As electrons flow from left to right through the electrode and wire, nitrate ions (anions) pass through the porous plug on the left into the copper(II) nitrate solution. The NO
ions neutralize the charge on the Cu
ions that are added to the solution as the copper metal is oxidized. At the same time, sodium ions (cations) move through the porous plug on the right and into the silver nitrate solution. The Na

ions “replace” the silver ions that leave the solution as they are reduced to silver metal, keeping the beaker on the right electrically neutral. Without the salt bridge, the compartments would not remain electrically neutral and no significant current would flow. However, if the two compartments are in direct contact, a salt bridge is not necessary.
The instant the circuit is completed, the voltmeter reads +0.46 V; this is called the
cell potential
The measure of the voltage (electrical potential difference) between the two electrodes of an electrochemical cell; indicates the cell's ability to produce an electric current.

. The cell potential is created when the two dissimilar metals are connected. It is a measure of the energy per unit charge available from the redox reaction. The volt (V) is the derived SI unit for electrical potential.
